content: Benznidazole is a nitroimidazole antimicrobial agent approved by the FDA for the treatment of Chagas disease (American trypanosomiasis), which is caused by the parasite Trypanosoma cruzi. Common adverse reactions associated with its use include abdominal pain, rash, weight loss, headache, nausea, vomiting, neutropenia, urticaria, pruritus, eosinophilia, and decreased appetite. Adult Indications and Dosage FDA-Labeled Indications and Dosage (Adult): Limited information is available regarding FDA-approved indications and dosage for adults in the drug label. Off-Label Use and Dosage (Adult): Limited information is available regarding off-label guideline-supported or non-guideline-supported use and dosage for adults in the drug label. Pediatric Indications and Dosage FDA-Labeled Indications and Dosage (Pediatric): Benznidazole is indicated for pediatric patients aged 2 to 12 years for the treatment of Chagas disease caused by T. cruzi. This indication was approved under accelerated approval based on the number of treated patients who became immunoglobulin G (IgG) antibody-negative against recombinant antigens of T. cruzi. Continued approval may depend on confirmatory trials verifying clinical benefit. The total daily dose for pediatric patients is 5 mg/kg to 8 mg/kg, administered orally in two divided doses approximately 12 hours apart, for a duration of 60 days. Off-Label Use and Dosage (Pediatric): Limited information is available regarding off-label guideline-supported or non-guideline-supported use and dosage for pediatric patients in the drug label. Contraindications Hypersensitivity: Benznidazole is contraindicated in patients with a history of hypersensitivity reactions to benznidazole or other nitroimidazole derivatives. Severe skin and soft tissue reactions have been reported. Disulfiram: Benznidazole is contraindicated in patients who have taken disulfiram within the last two weeks due to the risk of psychotic reactions when used concurrently. Alcohol and Propylene Glycol Products: Consumption of alcoholic beverages or products containing propylene glycol is contraindicated during and for at least three days after therapy with benznidazole. A disulfiram-like reaction (e.g., abdominal cramps, nausea, vomiting, headache, flushing) may occur due to the interaction between alcohol or propylene glycol and benznidazole. Warnings Genotoxicity: Benznidazole has demonstrated genotoxicity in humans, in vitro in bacterial and mammalian cell systems, and in vivo in rodents. Studies in pediatric patients with Chagas disease showed a two-fold increase in chromosomal aberrations and micronucleated lymphocytes after treatment with benznidazole. Carcinogenicity: Nitroimidazole agents structurally similar to benznidazole have been shown to be carcinogenic in mice and rats. It is unknown whether benznidazole is associated with carcinogenicity in humans. Fetal Harm: Based on animal studies, benznidazole can cause fetal harm when administered to pregnant women. Adverse effects observed in animal studies include ventricular septal defects, reduced maternal weight, smaller litter sizes, and abortions. Pregnant women should be advised of the potential risk to the fetus, and pregnancy testing is recommended for females of reproductive potential. Effective contraception should be used during treatment and for five days after the last dose. Serious Skin Reactions: Severe skin and subcutaneous disorders, including acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP), toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), erythema multiforme, and eosinophilic drug reactions, have been reported. Treatment should be discontinued at the first sign of these reactions. Neurological Effects: Benznidazole can cause paresthesia or symptoms of peripheral neuropathy, which may take several months to resolve. Headache and dizziness have also been reported. Neurological symptoms typically occur late in the course of treatment, and therapy should be discontinued immediately if they develop. Hematological Effects: Bone marrow depression, including neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia, and leukopenia, has been reported and resolved after treatment discontinuation. Patients with hematological manifestations should only take benznidazole under strict medical supervision, with regular monitoring of complete blood counts. Adverse Reactions Clinical Trials Experience: Adverse reactions observed in clinical trials include abdominal pain, rash, weight loss, headache, nausea, vomiting, decreased appetite, and increased transaminases. In pediatric patients, the most frequently reported adverse reactions were abdominal pain (25%), rash (16%), weight loss (13%), and headache (7%). Skin lesions were reported in 11% of pediatric patients in one trial. Postmarketing Experience: Adverse reactions identified during postmarketing use include those reported with other formulations of benznidazole outside the United States. The frequency and causal relationship to drug exposure are not always reliably established. Drug Interactions Disulfiram: Psychotic reactions have been reported in patients taking disulfiram and nitroimidazole agents concurrently. Benznidazole should not be given to patients who have taken disulfiram within the last two weeks. Alcohol and Propylene Glycol Products: Consumption of alcohol or products containing propylene glycol during or after therapy with nitroimidazole agents may cause disulfiram-like reactions. Although no similar reactions have been reported with benznidazole, alcohol and propylene glycol should be avoided during and for at least three days after therapy. Use in Specific Populations Pregnancy: Benznidazole may cause fetal harm based on animal studies. Treatment during pregnancy is not recommended due to the risk of embryo-fetal toxicity. Acute symptomatic Chagas disease in pregnant women should be evaluated on a case-by-case basis, weighing the risks and benefits of treatment. Lactation: Breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment with benznidazole due to the potential for serious adverse reactions and transmission of Chagas disease. Pediatric Use: Safety and effectiveness have been established in pediatric patients aged 2 to 12 years. Data for patients below 2 years and above 12 years are not available. Geriatric Use: No specific FDA guidance exists for geriatric populations. Renal and Hepatic Impairment: The use of benznidazole has not been evaluated in patients with renal or hepatic impairment. Administration and Monitoring Administration: Benznidazole tablets can be prepared as a slurry for pediatric patients with body weight less than 30 kg. Monitoring includes improvement of Chagas disease symptoms and regular complete blood counts before, during, and after therapy. Pregnancy testing is recommended for females of reproductive potential prior to initiating therapy. Pharmacology Mechanism of Action: Benznidazole is a nitroimidazole antimicrobial agent. Pharmacokinetics: Absorption is comparable under fasting conditions. Protein binding is approximately 44-60%. The elimination half-life is about 13 hours. Benznidazole and its metabolites are excreted in urine and feces. The metabolism pathway is unknown. Nonclinical Toxicology Carcinogenesis and Mutagenesis: Nitroimidazoles structurally similar to benznidazole have been shown to be carcinogenic in animal studies. Benznidazole has demonstrated genotoxicity in vitro and in vivo. Animal Toxicology: Toxicity studies in animals have shown ultrastructural changes in various tissues and neurotoxicity in dogs. Neurological signs included ataxia, hyperreflexia, and nystagmus.
